en: The Great Exposition (Mahāniddesa):
Exposition of the Discourse on the Eight Huts (Guhaṭṭhakasuttaniddesa), Chapter Two: The Section on the Eights (Aṭṭhakavagga)
Now he will explain the exposition of the Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta:
A being in this cave, covered by many [veils],
stands as a man plunged into delusion.
For such a person is indeed far from seclusion;
for sensual desires in the world are not easily abandoned.
The being in this cave is beset by many things.
For although it is said, "a being," the cave must first be described.
The cave is called the body.

Whether it be called "body" (kāya), "cave" (guhā), "deha," "sandeha," "boat" (nāvā), "chariot" (ratha), "banner" (dhaja), "anthill" (vammika), "city" (nagara), "nest" (nīḷa), "hut" (kuṭī), "tumor" (gaṇḍa), "pot" (kumbha), or "elephant" (nāga)—this is a designation for the body.
"Stuck in the cave" means stuck in the cave— clinging, attached, fastened, held, bound, and obstructed.
Just as a boil might be stuck, clinging, attached, fastened, held, and obstructed on a wall or on a peg,
even so he is stuck in the cave— clinging, attached, fastened, held, bound, and obstructed.
For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Rādha, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever engagement and clinging, mental standpoints, adherences, and underlying tendencies there are regarding form—in that one is stuck, in that one is deeply stuck;
therefore one is called ‘a being.’”
Regarding feeling, Rādha … regarding perception,
Rādha … regarding volitional formations, Rādha …

“Rādha, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever engagement and clinging, mental standpoints, adherences, and underlying tendencies there are in relation to consciousness—one is stuck there, one is deeply attached there.
Therefore, one is called ‘a being.
‘A being’ is a designation for being stuck.”
A being in the cave.

"Shrouded by much" means shrouded by many defilements: shrouded by lust, shrouded by hatred, shrouded by delusion, shrouded by anger, shrouded by resentment, shrouded by contempt, shrouded by domineering, shrouded by envy, and shrouded by stinginess.
Covered by deceit, covered by guile, covered by obstinacy, covered by aggression, covered by conceit, covered by arrogance,
covered by intoxication, covered by negligence— he is covered by all defilements.
from all forms of misconduct … from all anxieties … from all fevers …
“Enveloped, shrouded,
covered, veiled, enclosed, shut in, barred, concealed, and closed up by all forms of torment... by all unwholesome volitional formations—
thus is the being ‘enveloped in many ways’ within the cave.”
"A man standing, immersed in delusion": a man standing [in this way] stands by reason of lust when he is lustful;

he stands by reason of hatred when he is hateful; he stands by reason of delusion when he is deluded; he stands by reason of conceit when he is bound up; he stands by reason of views when he is misapprehending;
he stands by reason of restlessness when he has fallen into distraction; he stands by reason of doubt when he has fallen into uncertainty.
It persists; it persists by way of its latent tendency (*anusaya*).
Thus does a person persist.
For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Bhikkhus, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them, [he is bound].
There are, bhikkhus, sounds cognizable by the ear… odors cognizable by the nose… [tastes cognizable by the tongue…]”
Tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body...

mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust—if a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains clinging to them.”
Thus does a person persist.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, consciousness persists when it has a basis in form; with form as its object, form as its support, and being sprinkled with delight, it comes to growth, increase, and abundance.”
“Bhikkhus, consciousness, when it persists,

persists by having feeling as its means, or perception as its means, or volitional formations as its means; with volitional formations as its object, with volitional formations as its support, and being sprinkled with delight, it reaches growth, increase, and abundance.”
Even so does a person remain.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, if there is lust for physical nutriment, if there is delight in it, if there is craving for it, consciousness becomes established there and comes to growth."
Wherever consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form.
Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of volitional formations.
Where there is the growth of volitional formations, there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
“Where there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there is birth, aging, and death in the future.
Where there is birth, aging, and death in the future, I say, monks, that it is accompanied by sorrow, accompanied by dust, and accompanied by despair.
Thus does a person remain.
“Bhikkhus, if there is lust for the nutriment contact,

if there is delight, if there is craving— then consciousness becomes established there and grows. If there is lust for the nutriment mental volition… if there is lust for the nutriment consciousness, if there is delight, if there is craving— then consciousness becomes established there and grows.”
Wherever consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form.
Wherever there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of volitional formations.
Wherever there is the growth of volitional formations, there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
“Where there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there is birth, aging, and death in the future.
Where there is birth, aging, and death in the future, I say that it is accompanied by sorrow, dust, and despair, monks.
Thus does a person remain.
"He is immersed in delusion.
By "delusions" are meant the five strands of sensual pleasure:
forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; [and likewise sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects].
sounds cognizable by the ear … odors cognizable by the nose … flavors cognizable by the tongue …

Tangible objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust—for what reason are these five strands of sensual pleasure called "delusive"?
Because for the most part gods and humans are deluded, utterly deluded, and completely deluded by the five strands of sensual pleasure; being thus deluded...
Bewildered, utterly deluded, blinded by ignorance, obstructed, shrouded, enveloped, blocked, concealed, and covered—
therefore the five strands of sensual pleasure are called "delusions.
"Plunged into delusion" means plunged into delusion, deeply plunged, and submerged.
"A man who stands immersed in delusion is indeed far from seclusion.
As for "seclusion," there are three kinds of seclusion: [the seclusion of body, mind, and wisdom].
Physical seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion from acquisitions.
What is physical seclusion?
Here, a bhikkhu resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
He dwells secluded from the body.
He goes alone, stands alone, sits alone, lies down alone, enters the village alone for alms,
returns alone, sits alone in seclusion, undertakes walking meditation alone, and wanders alone.
He dwells, moves about, conducts himself, protects, maintains, and sustains [himself].
This is physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*).
What is mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*)?
The mind of one who has attained the first jhāna is secluded from the hindrances.
The mind of one who has attained the second jhāna is secluded from applied and sustained thought.
The mind of one who has attained the third jhāna is secluded from rapture.
For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, the mind is secluded from pleasure and pain.
For one who has attained the base of infinite space, the mind is secluded from the perception of form, the perception of sensory resistance, and the perception of diversity.
For one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, the mind is secluded from the perception of the base of infinite space.
For one who has attained the base of nothingness, the mind is secluded from the perception of the base of infinite consciousness.
For one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the mind is secluded from the perception of the base of nothingness.

For a stream-enterer, the mind is secluded from personality-belief, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and from the defilements associated with them.

In the once-returner, the gross fetter of sensual lust and the fetter of aversion, the gross underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion, and the defilements associated with them, have been removed from the mind.

In the non-returner, the residual fetter of sensual lust and the fetter of aversion, the residual underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion, and the defilements associated with them, have been removed from the mind.

For an Arahant, the mind is secluded from lust for the fine-material and immaterial realms, from conceit, restlessness, ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, the underlying tendency to ignorance, and from the defilements associated with these, as well as from all external signs.
This is seclusion of mind.
What is seclusion of acquisitions?
"Bases" (upadhi) are said to be the defilements, the aggregates, and volitional formations.
"Seclusion from bases" (upadhiviveka) is said to be the deathless Nibbāna—
that which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all bases, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nibbāna.

This is seclusion from the substrata (*upadhiviveka*). There is seclusion of body for those whose bodies are secluded and who delight in renunciation; seclusion of mind for those with purified minds who have attained supreme clarity; and seclusion from the substrata for persons free from substrata who have reached the cessation of formations (*visaṅkhāra*).
"Seclusions are far apart" means this.
This being who is thus in the cave, thus covered by many defilements, thus plunged into delusion—
he is far from seclusion of body, far from seclusion of mind, and far, very far, extremely far from seclusion of acquisitions;
he is not near, not nearby, not close, nor within reach of seclusion.
"Of such a kind" means one who is like that, established in that way, of that nature, and resembling that—namely, one who has plunged into delusion;
for such a person is far from seclusion.
Indeed, sensual pleasures in the world are not easy to abandon.
Regarding "sensual pleasures" (kāmā), in brief there are two kinds of sensual pleasure:
sensual pleasures as objects (vatthukāmā) and sensual pleasures as defilements (kilesakāmā).
What are sensual pleasures as objects?
Pleasant forms, pleasant sounds, pleasant smells, pleasant tastes, pleasant tangibles;
rugs, coverlets, female and male slaves; goats, sheep, chickens, pigs, elephants, cattle, horses, and mares; fields, lands, bullion, gold;
villages, towns, royal capitals, kingdoms, and provinces; treasuries and storehouses—whatever [there may be].
Any object that is provocative of lust—these are sensual pleasures as objects (*vatthukāmā*).

Furthermore, there are past sensual pleasures, future sensual pleasures, and present sensual pleasures; internal sensual pleasures, external sensual pleasures, and both internal and external sensual pleasures.

Sensual pleasures: inferior sensual pleasures, middling sensual pleasures, superior sensual pleasures; sensual pleasures leading to states of deprivation, human sensual pleasures, divine sensual pleasures;
present sensual pleasures, created sensual pleasures, uncreated sensual pleasures, those belonging to the realm of others' creations; possessed sensual pleasures, unpossessed sensual pleasures;
cherished sensual pleasures, uncherished sensual pleasures—all phenomena pertaining to the sense-sphere as well.
Phenomena belonging to the fine-material sphere, all phenomena belonging to the immaterial sphere, and those things which are the basis for craving and the objects of craving—
in the sense of being desirable, in the sense of being provocative of passion, and in the sense of being intoxicating—
these are called sensual objects as bases (*vatthukāmā*).
What are sensual desires as defilements?
Desire is sensual desire; lust is sensual desire; the lust of desire is sensual desire; intention is sensual desire; the lust of intention is sensual desire;

whatever in relation to sensual pleasures is longing for sensual pleasures, lust for sensual pleasures, delight in sensual pleasures, craving for sensual pleasures, affection for sensual pleasures, fever for sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures.
Clinging to sensual pleasures, the flood of sensual pleasures, the yoke of sensual pleasures, clinging to sensual pleasures, and the hindrance of sensual desire.
“I have seen your root, O sensual pleasure:
you are born from intentions.”
"I shall not intend that;
thus, O desire, you shall not exist.
These are called the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*).
“World” means the world of the lower realms, the world of humans, the world of devas; the world of the aggregates, the world of the elements, the world of the sense bases.
For sensual pleasures in the world are not easily abandoned.

Indeed, sensual pleasures in the world are difficult to abandon, difficult to give up, difficult to relinquish, difficult to subdue, difficult to disentangle, difficult to unravel, difficult to cross over, difficult to traverse, difficult to transcend, and difficult to turn away from.
For sensual pleasures in the world are indeed not easy to abandon.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“An embodied being, shrouded within the cave by many [defilements],”
A man who remains submerged in delusion is far indeed from seclusion,
for sensual pleasures in this world are not easily abandoned.
With desire as their cause, bound by attachment to existence,
they are difficult to liberate, for they are not released by another;
looking back and forth, both behind and before.
"Chanting for these very sensual pleasures or those of the past—
these are rooted in desire and bound by the gratification of existence. Here,
"desire" (icchā) is said to be craving (taṇhā).
Whatever lust, infatuation, inclination, compliance, delight, and lustful delight there is; infatuation of the mind;

desire, infatuation, cleaving, greed, obsession, attachment, the mire, the urge, deceit, the mother, the progenitor, the seamstress, the netter, the stream, the addiction, the thread, the spread, the drag, the companion, the aspiration, the guide to existence, the forest, the thicket, the haunt, the affection, and the regard.
Bondage, hope, longing, the state of longing; hope for forms, hope for sounds, hope for odors, hope for tastes, hope for tangibles; hope for gain, hope for wealth, hope for sons, hope for life;

yearning, intense yearning, excessive yearning, the act of yearning, the state of having yearned, greed, the practice of greed, the state of having practiced greed, hankering after what is desired, the desire for excellence, unrighteous passion, and improper avarice.
Inclination, longing, aspiration, desire, yearning; craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, craving for non-existence;
craving for form, craving for the formless, craving for cessation; craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, craving for mental phenomena;
a flood, a yoke, a tie, clinging, an obstruction, a hindrance, a covering, a bond, an affliction.
The underlying tendency, the obsession, the creeper, the craving, the root of suffering, the source of suffering, the origin of suffering, the snare of Māra, the trap of Māra,
the domain of Māra, the river of craving, the net of craving, the whirlpool of craving, the ocean of craving, covetousness, greed, and the unwholesome root.

"With longing as their source" means having longing as their source, having longing as their cause, having longing as their condition, having longing as their reason, and having longing as their origin.
With desire as their cause, they are bound by the pleasure of existence. There is one pleasure of existence: [the pleasure of sensual existence].
Pleasant feeling.
There are two kinds of gratification in existence:
pleasant feeling and agreeable objects.
Three things that are dear to existence:
youth, health, and life.
Four things that are dear to existence:
Gain, fame, praise, and pleasure.
The five gratifications of existence: agreeable forms, [agreeable sounds, agreeable odors, agreeable tastes, and agreeable tangibles].
agreeable sounds,
agreeable odors,
agreeable tastes,
Pleasant tactile objects.
The six bases of existence:
the possession of the eye, and so forth.
perfection of the ear,
perfection of the nose,
perfection of the tongue,
Perfection of body,
perfection of mind;
bound by delight in existence.
Bound to pleasant feeling,
bound to a desirable object,
bound to youth;
Bound to health,
bound to life,
bound to gain,
Bound by fame,
bound by praise,
bound by pleasure.
Bound to agreeable forms,
sounds,
and odors.
Bound by pleasant tastes, bound by pleasant tactile objects,
bound by the perfection of the eye, [and] the ear.
nose,
tongue,
body,

"Bound by the perfection of the mind, bound up, fettered, stuck, clinging, and entangled"—this means they are bound by the gratification of existence, having craving as their source. They are difficult to release, for there is no liberation other than this;
or else, those bases for the gratification of existence are difficult to release, or beings are difficult to free from them.
How are these bases for existence difficult to relinquish?
Pleasant feeling is difficult to relinquish;
a desirable object is difficult to relinquish.
Youth is difficult to relinquish,
health is difficult to relinquish,
and life is difficult to relinquish.
Gain is hard to relinquish,
fame is hard to relinquish,
and praise is hard to relinquish.
Pleasure is difficult to relinquish;
agreeable forms are difficult to relinquish;
agreeable sounds are difficult to relinquish.
Odors,
tastes,
and tactile objects are difficult to relinquish.
The perfection of the eye is difficult to relinquish;
so too the ear and the nose.

The perfection of the tongue, the body, and the mind are difficult to release, difficult to liberate, difficult to set free, difficult to disentangle, difficult to unbind; they are hard to cross over, hard to traverse, hard to transcend, and hard to turn back from.
Thus these bases for the flood of existence are difficult to abandon.
How is it that beings are hard to release from this?
Beings are hard to release from pleasant feeling.
Difficult to release from a desired object,
difficult to release from youth,
difficult to release from health.
Life is difficult to relinquish;
gain is difficult to relinquish;
fame is difficult to relinquish.
Praise is difficult to relinquish;
pleasure is difficult to relinquish;
and agreeable forms are difficult to relinquish.
With delightful sounds,
scents, and tastes.
Difficult to release from tangible objects,
difficult to release from the perfection of the eye,
[and] the ear.
The nose,
the tongue,
the body...

Through the perfection of the mind, it is difficult to release, difficult to lift up, difficult to extricate, difficult to raise, difficult to arouse, difficult to disentangle, difficult to unravel, difficult to cross over, difficult to traverse, difficult to transcend, and difficult to turn back from. Thus,
beings are difficult to release from this state— therefore, they are "difficult to liberate."
For those who do not seek liberation for others—being themselves mired in the mire—are unable to pull out another who is mired in the mire.
Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One:
"Cunda, it is impossible that one who is himself mired in the mire should pull out another who is mired in the mire."

“Indeed, Cunda, it is impossible that one who is himself undisciplined, untamed, and not fully extinguished (aparinibbuta) should discipline another, train another, or lead another to full extinction.
Thus, there is no liberation through another;
or rather, there is no other who can liberate.
If they should release them, then by one's own power, by one's own strength, by one's own energy, by one's own exertion, by one's own human power,
by one's own human strength, by one's own human energy, and by one's own human exertion, one should practice for oneself the right way,
the conformable way, the non-opposing way, the appropriate way, and the way that accords with the Dhamma.
"By practicing [the path], they might be liberated.
Thus, there is no liberation through another.
For this was also said by the Blessed One:
“I will not tolerate any kind of doubt in this world regarding liberation, O Dhota,
for I have realized the supreme Dhamma.”
"In this way, you shall cross over this flood.
Thus, there is indeed no liberation through another.
For it was also said by the Blessed One:
“By oneself indeed is evil done;
by oneself is one defiled.
By oneself is evil not done...”
One is purified by oneself alone;
purity and impurity are personal;
no one can purify another.
Thus too, there is no liberation through another.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“In the same way, brahmin, Nibbāna remains, the path leading to Nibbāna remains, and I remain as the one who encourages others.”
"And yet, when my disciples are thus advised and thus instructed by me, some attain the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, while others do not.
What can I do in this matter, brahmin?
The Tathāgata, brahmin, is merely the proclaimer of the path."
“The Buddha proclaims the path;
by practicing it themselves, they shall be liberated.
Thus, there is no liberation through another.
They are difficult to release, for they are not liberated by another.
"Looking back and forth"— here,
"back" refers to the future, and "forth" refers to the past.
Moreover, the future and the present are subsequent to the past; the past and the present are prior to the future.
How does one look back to what is prior?
One brings about delight therein, thinking: "Such was my form in the past."
“I had such feeling...
I had such perception...
I had such volitional formations...”
"I had such-and-such consciousness in the past"—in this regard, one takes delight.
In this way, too, one looks back to the past.
Or else: "Such was my eye in the past, such were the forms."
Therein, consciousness is bound by desire and lust.
Because consciousness is bound by desire and lust, one delights in that.
Delighting in that, one thus forms an expectation for the future.
“Thus was my ear in the past, thus were sounds”; ...
“Thus was my nose in the past, thus were odors”; ...
“Thus was my tongue in the past, thus were flavors”; ...
“Such was my body in the past, such were the tactile objects”—
and “such was my mind in the past, such were the mental phenomena”—
in this regard, consciousness is bound by desire and lust.
Because consciousness is bound by sensual lust, one delights in that.
Delighting in it, one thus forms expectations regarding the past.
Or else, one relishes those former instances of laughing, talking, and playing with women; one craves them and finds satisfaction therein.
In this way, one forms an expectation for the future. How does one form an expectation for the past?
One brings forth delight in the thought: "May I be of such a form in the future."
“May I have such feeling… may I have such perception… may I have such volitional formations….”
“May I have such consciousness in the future”—thus one finds delight therein.
In this way, one forms an expectation for the future.
Or else: “May my eye be thus in the future, may visible forms be thus.”
One sets the mind on the attainment of what has not yet been attained.
With the condition of that mental aspiration, one takes delight in it.
Taking delight in it, one also forms an expectation for the future.
“Thus may my ear be in the future time, thus sounds”;
… “thus may my nose be in the future time, thus odors”;
… “thus may my tongue be in the future time, thus tastes”; …
“May my body be thus in the future; may tangibles be thus”—...
“May my mind be thus in the future; may mental phenomena be thus”—he directs his mind toward the attainment of what has not yet been attained.
Conditioned by the mental aspiration, one delights in that.
Delighting in that, one also forms an expectation for the future, thinking:
"By means of this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, may I become a deva or some other kind of deva."
One sets the mind on the attainment of what has not yet been attained.
Due to that mental aspiration, one delights in it.
Delighting in it, one thus forms an expectation for the future.
Looking back and forth, they crave these very same sensual pleasures, whether past or future.
They long for these present sensual pleasures— the five strands of sense pleasure— desiring them, relishing them, longing for them, yearning for them, and craving them intensely.
"Or they long for the former": longing for, yearning for, and intensely craving the five strands of sensual pleasure that have passed away—these very desires are "longing for the former.
Thus the Blessed One said.
“Bound by the cause of desire and tied to the pleasure of existence,
they are difficult to liberate, for there is no release through another;
looking back or forward, they remain entangled.”
“Lusting after these very sensual pleasures or those of the past.
Greedy for sensual pleasures, addicted and deluded,
they are incapable of giving and settled upon what is uneven.
Brought to suffering, they lament:
"What shall we become when we have passed away from here?
We were greedy for sensual pleasures, addicted, and deluded."
Regarding "sensual pleasures" (kāmā): in brief, there are two kinds of sensual pleasure—sensual pleasure as objects (vatthukāmā) and sensual pleasure as defilements (kilesakāmā).
… [as follows] … these are called sensual pleasure as objects. … [as follows] …
These are called the defilements of sensual desire.
Greed is said to be craving;
it is that which is lust, infatuation, covetousness, and greed—the root of unwholesomeness.

"Greedy for sensual pleasures" means: those who, through the desire for defilements, are attached to sense-objects, infatuated, obsessed, maddened, clinging, stuck, and entangled—these are "greedy for sensual pleasures. "Devoted to sensual pleasures" means:

even those who seek, search for, and pursue sensual pleasures, whose conduct is such, who are abundant in that, who hold it dear, who are inclined toward it, prone to it, leaning toward it, intent upon it, and dominated by it—they too are "devoted to sensual pleasures."
Furthermore, through craving, they seek, search for, and pursue forms...
sounds... smells... [tastes... tactile objects.
In tastes...
in tangibles... [and so on]...

they seek them; they are devoted to that, frequent it, hold it as important, are inclined toward it, tend toward it, lean toward it, are intent upon it, and have it as their governing principle; they too are addicted to sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, those who acquire forms through craving ...
sounds ...
odors ... [tastes ... tangibles].

They obtain tastes... and tangibles, being devoted to them, frequenting them, regarding them as important, inclined toward them, leaning toward them, tending toward them, intent upon them, and dominated by them; they too are addicted to sensual pleasures.
And those who enjoy forms through the influence of craving...
In sounds … in odors … in tastes …

They enjoy tactile objects, being habituated to them, devoted to them, cherishing them, inclined toward them, leaning toward them, bent toward them, intent upon them, and dominated by them; they too are addicted to sensual pleasures.
Just as a quarrelsome person is addicted to quarreling, a laborer is addicted to labor, one wandering for alms is addicted to his range, and a meditator is addicted to meditation;

even so, those who seek, search for, and pursue sensual pleasures—being habituated to them, devoted to them, cherishing them, inclined toward them, leaning toward them, bent toward them, intent upon them, and dominated by them—they too are addicted to sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, by way of craving, they seek, search for, and pursue forms...
sounds... smells... [tastes... tactile objects... mental phenomena.
In tastes … in tangibles … [and so on] … they seek them;

they are devoted to that, frequent it, regard it as important, are inclined toward it, tend toward it, lean toward it, are intent upon it, and have it as their dominant influence; they too are addicted to sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, they acquire forms through craving ... sounds ... smells ... [tastes ... tangibles ... mental objects].

They experience tastes ... and tangibles, being devoted to them, frequenting them, cherishing them, leaning toward them, inclining toward them, tending toward them, intent upon them, and dominated by them; they too are addicted to sensual pleasures.
And those who enjoy forms through the influence of craving...
In sounds … in odors … in tastes …

They enjoy tangible objects; they are devoted to them, habituated to them, intent upon them; they are inclined toward them, prone to them, leaning toward them, dedicated to them, and dominated by them.
They too are addicted to sensual pleasures. "Confused" means that for the most part gods and humans are deluded, utterly deluded, thoroughly deluded by the five strands of sensual pleasure;
they are deluded, utterly deluded, thoroughly deluded, blinded by ignorance, obstructed, covered, enveloped, shut in, and concealed.
“Greedy for sensual pleasures, addicted, and deluded;
they are unrefined, settled in what is uneven. Regarding “unrefined” (*avadāniya*):

they are called “unrefined” because they do not understand (*ava-gacchanti*); they are also called “unrefined” because they are miserly; that is, they do not accept the words, the mode of expression, the teaching, or the instruction of the Buddhas and their disciples.
"Those who go to destruction. How do they go to destruction?
They go to hell, they go to the animal realm, they go to the sphere of hungry ghosts; thus they go to destruction.
They are stingy.
How are those who are stingy said to be "unfit for giving"?
There are five kinds of stinginess:
Stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding praise, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma.

Whatever such stinginess there is—stinginess, the act of being stingy, the state of being stingy, avarice, miserliness, harshness, and the state of the mind being ungrasping—this is called stinginess.

Furthermore, stinginess regarding the aggregates (khandhas) is also stinginess; stinginess regarding the elements (dhātus) is also stinginess; stinginess regarding the sense bases (āyatanas) is also stinginess—it is grasping.
This is called stinginess.
Because of this stinginess, people who are characterized by a lack of generosity become heedless.
Thus, those who are stingy are said to be ungenerous.
How is it that they do not accept the words, the mode of expression, the teaching, and the instruction of the Buddhas and their disciples—
that is, being "incapable"? They do not accept, nor do they wish to hear, the words, the mode of expression, the teaching, and the instruction of the Buddhas and their disciples.
They do not lend an ear; they do not establish a mind intent on understanding; they are disobedient, do not act upon what is said, and behave contrarily;
they turn their faces away.
Thus, because they do not take to heart the words, the manner of speech, the teaching, and the instruction of the Buddhas and their disciples, they are called "unworthy."
They are unworthy of offerings.
"Established in what is uneven" means they are established in uneven bodily action and established in uneven verbal action.
They are intent upon unwholesome mental action,
intent upon the unwholesome taking of life,
and intent upon the unwholesome taking of what is not given.
They are settled in unrighteous sexual misconduct,
settled in unrighteous false speech,
[and settled] in unrighteous divisive speech...
They are settled in uneven and harsh speech… in uneven idle chatter… in uneven covetousness.
They are settled in unwholesome ill will...
they are settled in unwholesome wrong view,
settled in unwholesome formations.
They are settled in the five uneven strands of sensual pleasure;
they are settled, deeply settled, established, attached, approached, clung to, intent upon, stuck, fastened, and obstructed by the five uneven hindrances.
Thus, being settled in the uneven, they are unfit for cleansing.
"Afflicted by suffering, they lament.
"Afflicted by suffering" means having reached suffering, having encountered suffering, having come upon suffering;
having reached Māra, having encountered Māra, having come upon Māra.
"Reached death, arrived at death, come upon death. "Lamenting" means they speak,
they prattle on, they grieve, they weary, they lament, they beat their breasts, they wail, and they fall into delusion—
thus, being brought to suffering, they lament.
"What shall we become after passing away from here? means: having passed away from here, what shall we become?
We shall become denizens of hell;
we shall become those born in the animal realm.
We shall become beings in the realm of hungry ghosts,
we shall become human beings,
we shall become gods.
"We shall be possessed of form;
we shall be formless;
we shall be percipient."
“Shall we be non-percipient?
Shall we be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient?
Shall we indeed exist in the future?”
"Will we indeed exist in the future? What will we be in the future? How will we be in the future?"
"What having been, shall we indeed become in the future time?"— thus, overcome by doubt, overcome by perplexity, fallen into uncertainty, they prattle and chatter,
they grieve, they weary, they lament, they beat their breasts, they wail, and they fall into confusion, saying:
"What indeed shall we become when we have passed away from here?"
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Greedy for sensual pleasures, addicted and deluded,
they are incapable of renunciation and settled upon the uneven path.”
"Afflicted by suffering, they lament:
'What shall we become when we have passed away from here?
Therefore, a person should train right here."
Whatever one may know to be unrighteous in the world,
for that reason one should not act unrighteously;
for the wise say this life is indeed short.
"Therefore, indeed, a person should train right here.
"Therefore" means for that reason, for that cause, for that condition, for that source; it means "therefore," seeing this danger in sensual pleasures.
"One should train" refers to the three trainings:
the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
What is the training in higher virtue?

Here, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.

The minor aggregate of virtue, the great aggregate of virtue—virtue as a foundation, as a beginning, as conduct, as restraint, as control, as liberation, as the foremost for the attainment of wholesome states:
this is the training in higher virtue.
What is the training in higher mind?

Here, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration.
With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: “He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness”; thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
This is the training in higher mind.
What is the training in higher wisdom?
Here, a bhikkhu is wise; he is endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
Thus one understands as it really is: “This is suffering”; one understands as it really is: “This is the origin of suffering”; one understands as it really is:
“This is the cessation of suffering”; one understands as it really is: “This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.”
“He understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it really is:
‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’”
This is the training in higher wisdom.
One should train by being mindful of these three trainings;
one should train by knowing them.
One should train while contemplating, one should train while reflecting,
and one should train while resolving the mind.
One should train while resolving with faith;
one should train while exerting energy;
one should train while establishing mindfulness.
One should train in concentrating the mind;
one should train in understanding with wisdom;
one should train in directly knowing that which is to be directly known.
One should train by fully understanding that which is to be fully understood;
one should train by abandoning that which is to be abandoned;
one should train by developing that which is to be developed.
Realizing that which is to be realized, one should train, practice, conduct oneself accordingly, and live having undertaken [the training].
"Herein" means: in this view, in this inclination, in this preference, in this adoption, in this Dhamma, in this Vinaya, in this Dhamma-Vinaya, in this dispensation, in this holy life.
"In this Teacher's Dispensation, in this very selfhood, in this human world"—therefore it is said "here.
"A person" means a being, a man... [and so on] ...a human being.
Therefore, let a person train right here in this world:
"Whatever one may know to be a danger in the world.
The phrase "whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*) is a term signifying the complete inclusion of everything—in every way, entirely, without remainder, and without exception.
"Whatever it may be":
"one should know what is uneven" means one should know that an uneven bodily action is uneven,
and one should know that an uneven verbal action is uneven.
One should know unwholesome mental action as unwholesome;
one should know the taking of life as unwholesome;
one should know the taking of what is not given as unwholesome.
One should know that sexual misconduct regarding sensual pleasures is uneven;
one should know that false speech is uneven;
one should know that malicious speech is uneven.
One should know harsh speech as uneven;
one should know frivolous chatter as uneven;
one should know covetousness as uneven.
One should know unwholesome ill will as unwholesome;
one should know wrong view as unwholesome;
one should know unwholesome volitional formations as unwholesome.
One should know the five strands of sensual pleasure as a peril;
one should know the five hindrances as a peril—one should understand them, discern them, penetrate them, and pierce through them.
"The world" refers to the world of the lower realms ... [and so on] ... the world of the sense bases.
"Whatever one might know to be unrighteous in the world,
one should not practice unrighteousness for its sake.
For the sake of unrighteous bodily action, one should not practice unrighteousness.
One should not act improperly for the sake of improper verbal action;
one should not act improperly for the sake of improper mental action;
one should not act improperly for the sake of the taking of life.
One should not act improperly for the sake of improper taking of what is not given;
one should not act improperly for the sake of improper sexual misconduct;
one should not act improperly for the sake of improper false speech.
For the sake of uneven and malicious speech, one should not act unfairly;
for the sake of uneven and harsh speech, one should not act unfairly;
for the sake of uneven idle chatter, one should not act unfairly.
For the sake of uneven covetousness, one should not act unfairly;
for the sake of uneven ill will, one should not act unfairly;
for the sake of uneven wrong view, one should not act unfairly.
One should not act improperly for the sake of improper volitional formations;
one should not act improperly for the sake of the five improper strands of sensual pleasure;
one should not act improperly for the sake of the five improper hindrances.
On account of an uneven volition, one should not act unevenly;
on account of an uneven aspiration, one should not act unevenly;

on account of an uneven resolve, one should not act unevenly—one should not practice it, should not engage in it, should not habitually practice it, nor should one continue in its observance after having undertaken it.
"One should not act unjustly for its sake;
for the wise say this life is but brief.
Here, "life" (*jīvita*) means vitality (*āyu*), persistence, subsistence, maintenance, movement, conduct, preservation, life itself, and the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
Moreover, life is short for two reasons:
either because its duration is limited, or because its inherent nature is limited. How is it that life is short because its duration is limited?
In the past moment of consciousness, one lived; one does not live, nor will one live.
In the future moment of consciousness, one will live; one does not live, nor did one live.
In the present moment of consciousness, one lives; one did not live, nor will one live.
“Life and the personal existence,
and all pleasure and pain, are joined together with a single mind.”
The moment passes swiftly.
Those gods who remain for eighty-four thousand aeons—
But even they do not truly live,
being conjoined with two minds:
those that have ceased and those of one who is dying.
Or for one remaining here,
all the aggregates are alike;
having passed away, they do not undergo rebirth-linking.
Those that have broken up in the immediate past,
those that will break up in the future,
and those that have ceased in the interval between them—
There is no irregularity in his characteristics.
He was not born by means of what has not yet arisen;
he lives by means of the present.
The world is broken by the mind;
it is merely a conventional designation for what is ultimately real.
It proceeds according to its own inclinations.
Directed by desire,
the streams flow unceasingly,
conditioned by the six sense bases.
Those who have not stored up merit are broken and gone;
there is no accumulation for the future.
And those who have been reborn and remain—
Like a mustard seed on the tip of an awl,
the destruction of arisen phenomena precedes their appearance.
Things subject to dissolution persist,
unmixed with those of the past;
they come from the unseen.
The formations pass away out of sight;
like the appearance of lightning in the sky,
they arise and then vanish.
Thus, life is short due to the brevity of its duration.
How is life short due to the brevity of its inherent nature?
Life is dependent on the in-breath; life is dependent on the out-breath; life is dependent on both the in-breath and the out-breath.
Life is bound up with the great primary elements; life is bound up with physical food;
life is bound up with heat; life is bound up with consciousness.
The root of these is weak, and their prior causes are also weak.
Those which are conditions are also weak; those which are productive are also weak.
Among these, the co-existent are weak, the associated are also weak, the conascent are also weak, and that which is the motivator is also weak. These are always weak in relation to one another;
these are unstable toward one another. These cause one another to fall; for there is no protection from one another, nor do these establish one another.
Even one who is being reborn is not found;
no one is diminished by anything at all,
for these gandhabbas are entirely non-existent.
These shine because of those who came before;
those who shine have themselves passed away long ago.
Both those of the past and those of the future—
“We have never seen one another.
Thus, life is brief due to its limited duration.
Furthermore, compared to the lifespan of the gods of the Four Great Kings, the life of humans is short and meager.
Life is short, life is momentary, life is fleeting, life is brief, life is not to be relied upon, life does not endure for long.
[This applies to] the gods of the Thirty-three... [and so on].
...of the Yāma devas...
of the Tusita devas...
of the Nimmānarati devas...
Compared to the lifespan of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas... and the Brahmakāyika devas, the lifespan of human beings is short,
limited, meager, momentary, fleeting, transient, and not enduring.
Life is of short duration.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, brief is the lifespan of human beings."
The future life must be traversed; it is to be understood through wisdom. What is wholesome must be done; the holy life must be lived. For one who is born, there is no escaping death.
Monks, he who lives long lives for a hundred years or a little more.
Short is the lifespan of human beings.
A good person would not despise him; one should walk as if with one's head on fire—
for there is no escaping death.
Days and nights pass by,
life comes to an end;
the lifespan of mortals is being exhausted.
"Like the water in mountain streams.
The wise say that this life is indeed short.

"The wise" (dhīra) means those who are steadfast; they are called wise because they possess fortitude, because they are endowed with fortitude, and because they have made their evil deeds wise [by abandoning them].
Wisdom (*dhī*) is called discernment (*paññā*).
That which is discernment, understanding, investigation, thorough investigation, investigation of phenomena, discernment of characteristics, close examination, close scrutiny,
sagacity, skill, proficiency, discrimination, reflection, examination, vastness, intelligence, guidance, and insight.

Clear comprehension is a goad; it is wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the lamp of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, the investigation of phenomena, and right view.
Because they are endowed with that wisdom, they are called the steadfast.
Moreover, they are wise regarding the aggregates, wise regarding the elements, wise regarding the sense bases, wise regarding dependent origination, wise regarding the foundations of mindfulness,
wise regarding the right efforts, wise regarding the bases of psychic power, wise regarding the faculties, wise regarding the powers, wise regarding the factors of enlightenment,
wise regarding the path, wise regarding the fruits, and wise regarding Nibbāna.
Those wise ones have said thus:
"The life of human beings is short, a limited life, a trifling life, a momentary life, a light life, a fleeting life, a non-eternal life, a life that does not endure for long.
Thus they have said, thus they speak, thus they declare, thus they illuminate, thus they express themselves.
The wise say this life is short.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, indeed, a person here should train..."
Whatever one may know to be unrighteous in the world,
for that reason one should not act unrighteously;
for the wise say this life is indeed short.
I see this generation in the world quivering,
overcome by craving for states of existence;
base men prattle in the jaws of death.
"Those who are not free from craving for various states of existence—I see them quivering in the world.

"I see": I see with the fleshly eye; I see with the divine eye; I see with the wisdom-eye; I see with the Buddha-eye; I see with the universal eye. I behold, I look upon, I contemplate, I meditate upon, and I examine.
“World” means the world of the lower realms, the world of humans, the world of devas, the world of the aggregates, the world of the elements,
and the world of the sense bases. “Trembling” means trembling with the trembling of craving and trembling with the trembling of views.
Trembling with the trembling of defilements,
trembling with the trembling of effort,
and trembling with the trembling of karmic result.
Trembling with the trembling of misconduct,
trembling with passion for what is lustful,
trembling with hatred for what is corrupted.
One who is deluded, wavering through delusion;
one who is bound, wavering through conceit;
one who is misapprehended, wavering through views.
That which has gone to distraction, quivering with restlessness;
that which has gone to what is undesirable, quivering with doubt;
and that which has become firmly rooted, quivering with underlying tendencies.
Trembling because of gain,
trembling because of loss,
trembling because of fame,
Trembling because of gain,
trembling because of praise,
trembling because of blame.
Trembling because of pleasure,
trembling because of pain,
trembling because of birth;
Trembling because of aging,
trembling because of illness,
trembling because of death.
trembling with sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
trembling with the suffering of hell;
trembling with the suffering of the animal realm;
Trembling with the suffering of the realm of hungry ghosts,
trembling with the suffering of the human realm,
and trembling with the suffering rooted in descent into the womb.
Trembling with the suffering rooted in remaining in the womb,
trembling with the suffering rooted in emerging from the womb,
and trembling with the suffering connected to being born.
One who is quivering with suffering caused by another,
quivering with suffering caused by one's own effort,
and quivering with suffering caused by the effort of another.
Trembling with the suffering of suffering,
trembling with the suffering of formations,
trembling with the suffering of change.
Trembling with the suffering of eye disease,
trembling with the suffering of ear disease,
trembling with the suffering of nose disease... [and so forth].
... by disease of the tongue ...
by disease of the body ...
by disease of the head ...
... by ear disease ...
by mouth disease ...
by tooth disease ...
... by coughing ...
by spitting ...
by nasal catarrh ...
... by burning fever ...
by old age ...
by abdominal disease ...
... to fainting ...
to dysentery ...
to colic ...
... by dysentery ...
by leprosy ...
by abscesses ...
... by leprosy ...
by consumption ...
by epilepsy ...
...daddu ...
kaṇḍu ...
kacchu ...
... with marrow ...
with a hair-comb ...
with blood ...
... by bile ...
by diabetes mellitus ...
to the shoulder ...
...a carbuncle ... a fistula ...
a disease originating from bile ...
by a disease arising from phlegm … by a disease arising from wind … by a disease arising from a combination [of the humors] …
...by an affliction arising from a change in the seasons ...
by an affliction arising from an irregular lifestyle ...
by an affliction resulting from external trauma ...
... by a disease born of the ripening of karma ...
by cold ...
by heat ...
Of hunger … of thirst … of excrement …
... by the suffering of urination ... by the suffering of contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping reptiles ...
by the suffering of a mother's death ...
by the suffering of a father’s death … by the suffering of a brother’s death … by the suffering of a sister’s death …
by the suffering of a son’s death … by the suffering of a daughter’s death … by the loss of kinsmen …
...by the misfortune of wealth,
...by the misfortune of illness,
...by the misfortune of moral conduct...
"I see, I behold, I look upon, I contemplate, I examine one who is quivering, trembling, shuddering, shaking, and convulsing due to the suffering of the calamity of views"—
thus, "I see this generation quivering in the world,
overcome by craving for states of existence."
“Pajā” is a designation for beings.
“Taṇhā” means craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena.
“Taṇhāgataṃ” means gone with craving, followed by craving, permeated by craving, near to craving, fallen under the sway of craving, overcome, and possessed by craving.

"Regarding 'in states of existence' (bhavesu): this means in the sense-sphere existence, the fine-material existence, and the immaterial existence—in these states of existence, this generation is overcome by craving.
'Inferior men lament in the mouth of death.'"
“Base people” means: base people are so called because they are possessed of base bodily action;
base people are so called because they are possessed of base verbal action;
base people are so called because they are possessed of base mental action.
"Those endowed with inferior taking of life are inferior persons;
those endowed with inferior taking of what is not given...
those endowed with inferior sexual misconduct..."
By inferior false speech … by inferior malicious speech … by inferior harsh speech …
By low idle chatter … by low covetousness … by low ill will …
With inferior wrong view … with inferior formations … with inferior five strands of sensual pleasure and hindrances …
Those who possess inferior volition,
inferior aspiration,
and inferior resolve are called inferior persons— lowly, base, fallen away, mean, wretched, contemptible, inferior, and limited.
"Inferior men lament in the mouth of death.
"In the mouth of death" means in the mouth of Māra, in the mouth of death.
"Attained by death, overtaken by death, come under the sway of death;
attained by Māra, overtaken by Māra, come under the sway of Māra;

attained by dying, overtaken by dying, come under the sway of dying—they lament, they wail, they grieve, they weary, they lamentation, they beat their breasts, they cry out, and they fall into delusion."
"Inferior men lament in the mouth of death;
they are not free from craving for existence after existence. Here, "craving" refers to craving for form … [and so on] … up to craving for consciousness.
Craving for phenomena (*dhammatṛṣṇā*).

Regarding "in various states of existence" (*bhavābhavesu*): it means in various states of existence—namely, in the state of becoming through karma (*karmabhava*), in renewed existence (*punarbhava*), and in the state of sensual becoming (*kāma-bhava*);
in the state of karma, in the state of sensual becoming, in renewed existence, and in the state of form-becoming (*rūpa-bhava*).
In the existence of karma, in the existence of form, in renewed existence, and in the formless existence;
in the existence of karma and the formless existence, in renewed existence, in repeated existence,
in repeated destinies, in repeated rebirths, in repeated rebirth-linkings, and in the repeated manifestation of individuality.
They have not removed craving, they have not departed from craving, they have not cast off craving, they have not overcome craving.
They are not freed from craving, craving has not been abandoned, craving has not been relinquished— thus they are "those who have not removed craving" regarding existence after existence.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“I see this generation in the world quivering,
this folk gone astray through craving for states of existence.”
"Inferior men lament in the mouth of death,
for they have not freed themselves from craving for existence after existence.
Behold those things cherished as "mine" quivering with agitation!
Like a fish in water whose stream has run dry;
seeing even this, one should wander without the sense of "mine," not forming attachment to states of existence.
"Behold those who are possessed by 'mine' and are trembling.
"Possession by 'mine'" (mamatta) is twofold:
possession by craving (taṇhāmamatta) and possession by views (diṭṭhimamatta).
What is the measure of "mine" regarding craving?
Whatever is delimited, defined by boundaries, encompassed, limited, and grasped as "mine" by means of that which is called craving: "This is mine."
"This is mine,
this much is mine,
to this extent am I."
Forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles;

rugs and coverlets; female and male slaves; goats, sheep, chickens, and pigs; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares; fields and lands; bullion and gold; villages, towns, royal capitals, kingdoms, and provinces;
as well as the treasury and the storehouse—even the entire great earth—one regards as "mine" through the influence of craving.
To whatever extent there is the hundred-and-eightfold wandering of craving,
this is the measure of craving.
What is the measure of views?
The personality-belief view has twenty bases,
the false view has ten bases,
and the view of grasping at extremes has ten bases.
Any such view, a resort to views, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a distortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views, a seizing, a grasping,
an adherence, a misapprehension, a wrong path, a false course,

a state of error, a sectarian standpoint, a perverted seizing, a distorted seizing, a reversal of seizing, a wrong seizing— the seizing [of the thought]: "In what is not as it really is, there is what is as it really is."
"As far as the sixty-two types of views extend, this is merely a matter of views.
'Behold those who cherish what is theirs, trembling'— they tremble when their cherished object is threatened with loss,
and they tremble even when it is being taken away."
They quiver even when not cut;
they quiver being apprehensive of the change of the object they cherish as "mine";
and they quiver even while undergoing change.
Even when it has changed, they quiver, quiver strongly, quiver thoroughly, quiver intensely; they tremble, tremble strongly, tremble thoroughly.

"See them, behold them, look at them, contemplate them, examine them as they are thus quivering, quivering strongly, quivering thoroughly, quivering intensely, trembling, trembling strongly, trembling thoroughly"—thus, see them quivering in that which is cherished as "mine."
"Like fish in shallow water where the stream has run dry":
just as fish in shallow, limited water, when their supply of water is exhausted,
quiver, twitch, throb, and writhe while being pursued, snatched up, and devoured by crows, hawks, or cranes.
They tremble, they tremble violently, they tremble all over;
even so, people quiver when their cherished possession is threatened with being taken away,
and they quiver when it is actually being taken away.
They quiver even when not cut off;
they quiver out of fear of the change of a cherished object;
they quiver even while undergoing change.
"Even when things have changed, they quiver, throb, tremble, and shake; they flutter, flutter about, and flutter all over—like fish in shallow water where the stream has run dry.
Having seen this too, one should wander without the sense of "mine."
"Having seen this danger, having perceived it, weighed it, scrutinized it, clarified it, and made it manifest"—this is what is meant by "having seen even this.
"One should wander without 'mine-ness'"—as for "mine-ness," there are two kinds of mine-ness: [the mine-ness of craving and the mine-ness of views].
The intoxication of craving and the intoxication of views ...
[as above] ... this is the intoxication of craving ... [as above] ... this is the intoxication of views.
Having abandoned the conceit of craving and relinquished the conceit of views, he does not treat the eye as "mine," nor the ear, nor the nose, nor the tongue, nor the body,

nor the mind as "mine. He does not treat forms… sounds… smells… tastes… tangibles… mental phenomena… family… assemblies… dwellings… gains… fame… praise… pleasure… robes… almsfood… lodgings… or medicinal requisites for the sick as "mine."

the sense-sphere realm … the fine-material realm … the immaterial realm … existence in the sense sphere … existence in the fine-material sphere … existence in the immaterial sphere … existence with perception … existence without perception … existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception … one-constituent existence … four-constituent existence … five-constituent existence … the past … the future … the present …

"Not being possessive, not grasping, not clinging, and not adhering to phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, or cognized— one should walk, dwell, move, conduct oneself, protect, preserve, and maintain [oneself]"— having seen this too,
one should walk without possessiveness.
"Not forming attachment to states of existence."
"In existences" means in the existence of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*), the existence of form (*rūpabhava*), and the formless existence (*arūpabhava*).
"Attachment" is said to be craving (*taṇhā*).
It is that which is lust, infatuation... [as before] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
"Not forming attachment to states of existence" means:

not forming attachment to states of existence; not forming, not generating, not producing, not bringing forth, and not giving rise to desire, affection, lust, or longing for them—this is "not forming attachment to states of existence."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Behold those who are possessed by ‘mine,’ quivering like fish in a shallow stream with its current exhausted.”
"Having seen this as well,
one should wander without the sense of 'mine,' not forming attachment to states of existence;
having removed desire for both extremes."
Having fully understood contact, he is not attached to it;
not doing that which is censured by himself,
the wise one is not smeared by what is seen or heard.
"Having removed desire for both ends":
"Ends" means contact is one end and the origination of contact is the second end; the past is one end and the future is the second end;
pleasant feeling is one end and painful feeling is the second end; name is one end and form is the second end.
One extreme is the six internal sense bases; the second extreme is the six external sense bases. One extreme is personal existence (*sakkāya*);
the second extreme is the origin of personal existence.

"Sensual desire" refers to that which is sensual lust toward sense pleasures, sensual passion, sensual delight, sensual craving, sensual affection, sensual fever, sensual infatuation, sensual clinging, the flood of sensuality, the yoke of sensuality, the clinging to sensuality, and the hindrance of sensual lust.

"Having removed desire for both extremes": having removed, thoroughly removed, abandoned, dispelled, made to vanish, and brought to non-existence desire for both extremes—this is "having removed desire for both extremes.
"Not clinging after having fully understood contact."
Contact (phassa) is: eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, mind-contact;

contact of designation (adhivacana-samphassa), contact of resistance (paṭigha-samphassa); contact to be experienced as pleasant, contact to be experienced as painful, contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
wholesome contact, unwholesome contact, and indeterminate contact.
Contact: contact pertaining to the sense-sphere, contact pertaining to the fine-material sphere, contact pertaining to the immaterial sphere; empty contact, signless contact, wishless contact;
worldly contact, supramundane contact; past contact, future contact, present contact—whatever kind of contact there is, such as touching, contacting, the state of having contacted.
This is called contact.
"Having fully understood contact" means having fully understood contact by means of three kinds of full understanding:
full understanding as the known, full understanding as investigation, and full understanding as abandonment.
What is full understanding through knowledge?
One knows contact: "This is eye-contact; this is ear-contact; this is nose-contact; this is tongue-contact."
This is bodily contact; this is mental contact; this is conceptual contact; this is impingement contact;
this is contact to be experienced as pleasant; this is contact to be experienced as painful; this is contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
this is wholesome contact; this is unwholesome contact; this is indeterminate contact; this is of the sense-sphere realm.
He knows and sees: "This is contact pertaining to the realm of form; this is contact pertaining to the formless realm; this is empty contact; this is signless contact;
this is desireless contact; this is mundane contact; this is supramundane contact;
this is past contact; this is future contact; this is present contact."
This is full understanding through knowledge.
What is full understanding through scrutiny?
Having thus known it, one scrutinizes contact.
As impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as an arrow, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as a plague, as a disaster,
as a terror, as a menace, as unstable, as crumbling, as lacking refuge, as lacking shelter,
as lacking protection, as empty, as vain, as void, as non-self, as a danger, as subject to change, as coreless, as the root of calamity, as a murderer, and as destruction.
One scrutinizes it as being accompanied by taints, conditioned, the bait of Māra, subject to birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief,
and despair, subject to defilement, and as its origin, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape—
this is the full understanding through scrutiny.
What is full understanding as abandonment?
Having investigated in this way, one abandons desire and lust for contact; one dispels it, brings it to an end, and causes it to cease.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, abandon whatever desire and lust there is for contacts.
In this way, that contact will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and incapable of arising again in the future.
This is full understanding by abandoning.
"Having fully understood contact" means:
having thoroughly understood contact by means of these three kinds of full understanding.
"Without being attached" means: [not being greedy].
"Greed" is said to be craving.
It is that which is lust, infatuation... [as above] ...covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
One for whom this greed has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—he is called "free from greed."
Thus, he is not greedy for forms, not greedy for sounds, not greedy for odors, not greedy for tastes, not greedy for tangibles;
not greedy for clans, assemblies, dwellings, gains, fame, praise, pleasure, robes, almsfood, lodgings, or medicinal requisites for the sick;

not greedy for the realm of sense-desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm; not greedy for existence in the realm of sense-desire, existence in the realm of form, existence in the formless realm, existence in the realm of perception, existence in the realm of non-perception, or existence in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
In a one-constituent existence... in a four-constituent existence... in a five-constituent existence...
in the past... in the future... in the present...
regarding phenomena seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—being without greed, unattached, not infatuated, not clinging, and free from lust.
Free from greed, having abandoned greed, overcome greed, released from greed, relinquished greed, renounced greed;
free from lust, having abandoned lust, overcome lust, released from lust, relinquished lust, renounced lust;
hungerless, extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, he dwells with a self that has become sublime.
Having fully understood contact, he is not attached.
"That which one censures, not doing that"— the word "that" (*yad*) means "whatever."
"One who reproaches oneself" reproaches oneself for two reasons: on account of what has been done and on account of what has not been done.
How does one reproach oneself on account of what has been done and what has not been done?
"I have committed misconduct of body; I have not practiced good conduct of body"—thus one reproaches oneself.
"I have committed misconduct of speech; I have not practiced good conduct of speech"—thus one reproaches oneself.
One reproaches oneself:
"I have committed a mental misconduct; I have failed to perform a mental good deed"—thus one reproaches oneself.
"I have committed the taking of life; I have not practiced abstention from the taking of life"—thus he reproaches himself.
"I have committed the taking of what is not given; I have not practiced abstention from the taking of what is not given"—thus he reproaches himself.
One reproaches oneself:
"I have committed sexual misconduct; I have failed to abstain from sexual misconduct"—thus one reproaches oneself.
"I have committed false speech; I have not practiced abstention from false speech"—thus he reproaches himself.
"I have committed malicious speech; I have not practiced abstention from malicious speech"—thus he reproaches himself.
One reproaches oneself:
"Harsh speech was uttered by me; abstention from harsh speech was not practiced by me"—thus one reproaches oneself.
"Idle chatter has been committed by me; abstention from idle chatter has not been practiced by me"—thus he reproaches himself.
"Covetousness has been committed by me; non-covetousness has not been practiced by me"—thus he reproaches himself.
One reproaches oneself:
"I have practiced ill will; I have not practiced non-ill will"—thus one reproaches oneself.
"I have done wrong views; I have not done right view"—thus one reproaches oneself.
In this way, one reproaches oneself on account of what has been done and what has not been done.
Or else, he reproaches himself thus: "I am not one who fulfills the precepts";
"I have not guarded the doors of the sense faculties."
He reproaches himself:
"I am immoderate in food"—
thus he reproaches himself.
"One who is not devoted to wakefulness"—
thus he censures himself.
"One who is not endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension"— thus...
He blames himself:
"The four foundations of mindfulness were not developed by me"—
thus he blames himself.
"Four right efforts have not been developed by me"—
thus he reproaches himself.
"Four bases of psychic power have not been developed by me"— thus he reproaches himself.
He reproaches himself:
"The five faculties have not been developed by me"—
thus he reproaches himself.
"Five powers have not been developed by me"—
thus he reproaches himself.
"Seven factors of enlightenment have not been developed by me"— thus [he reproaches himself].
One reproaches oneself:
"The noble eightfold path has not been developed by me"—
thus one reproaches oneself.
"‘Suffering has not been fully understood by me’—
thus one reproaches oneself.
‘The origin has not been abandoned by me’— thus..."
One reproaches oneself:
"The path has not been developed by me"—
thus one reproaches oneself.
"Ceasing has not been realized by me"—
thus he reproaches himself.
In this way, he reproaches himself for what has been done and for what has not been done.
Thus, not performing, not producing, not generating, not causing to arise, and not causing to manifest that deed which is self-reproachable—
one who does not perform that which is self-reproachable,
the wise one, is not smeared by what is seen or heard.
There are two kinds of clinging:
the clinging of craving and the clinging of views... [as before] ...this is the clinging of craving... [as before] ...
This is the smear of views.
The "wise one" (dhīra) is one who is learned, possessed of wisdom, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious.

Having abandoned the smear of craving and relinquished the smear of views, the wise one does not smear himself on what is seen, does not smear himself on what is heard, does not smear himself on what is sensed, and does not smear himself on what is cognized; he does not smear himself, does not smear himself over, and does not smear himself all over.

"Unburnt, unscorched, and unsullied; having gone forth, escaped, and being liberated, he dwells with a mind free from boundaries and detached"—thus "the wise one is not smeared by what is seen or heard.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having removed desire for both ends,
having fully understood contact and being free from craving;
not doing that which leads to self-reproach— ”
“The wise one is not defiled by what is seen or heard.
Having fully understood perception, the sage crosses over the flood,
remaining undefiled amidst possessions.
With the arrow pulled out, wandering heedfully,
one would desire neither this world nor the next;
having fully understood perception, one should cross over the flood.

Perception: the perception of sensual desire, the perception of ill will, the perception of cruelty, the perception of renunciation, the perception of non-ill will, the perception of non-cruelty, the perception of forms, the perception of sounds, the perception of odors, the perception of tastes,
the perception of tangibles, and the perception of mental phenomena— whatever kind of perception there is, the act of perceiving, the state of having perceived— this is called perception.
"Thoroughly understanding perception" means having thoroughly understood perception by means of three kinds of thorough understanding:
thorough understanding as the known, thorough understanding as investigation, and thorough understanding as abandonment.
What is thorough understanding as the known?

He knows perception: “This is the perception of sensual desire; this is the perception of ill will; this is the perception of cruelty; this is the perception of renunciation; this is the perception of non-ill will; this is the perception of non-cruelty;
this is the perception of forms; this is the perception of sounds; this is the perception of odors; this is the perception of tastes.”
One knows and sees: "This is the perception of tangible objects; this is the perception of mental phenomena"—this is full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*).
What is full understanding through investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*)?
Having understood it thus, he brings his perception to its conclusion.

He brings it to its conclusion by way of impermanence, suffering, a disease, a tumor, a dart, a calamity, an affliction, alien, disintegrating, a plague, a disaster, a terror, a menace, unstable, perishable; ...
[and so on] ... by way of origin, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape.
This is full understanding by investigation.
What is full understanding by abandoning?
Having thus investigated, one abandons, dispels, and brings to non-existence desire and lust for perception.
For this was also said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, whatever desire and lust there is for perception, abandon it.
In this way, that perception will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and no longer subject to future arising.”
This is the full understanding as abandonment.

"One fully understands perception" means that having fully understood perception by means of these three kinds of full understanding, one would cross over the flood—the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance; one would cross over it, cross over it completely, cross over it thoroughly, transcend it, and pass beyond it.
Having fully understood perception, one should cross over the flood.
The sage is unstained by possessions.
"Possessions" means two kinds of possessions: [the internal and the external].
The appropriation of craving and the appropriation of views...
[as before] ...this is the appropriation of craving... [as before] ...this is the appropriation of views.
"A sage" (muni):
"Sageliness" (mona) is said to be knowledge (ñāṇa).
That which is wisdom, understanding ... [as above] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—it is one endowed with that knowledge who is a sage, one who has attained sageliness.
There are three types of nobility:
nobility of body, nobility of speech, and nobility of mind.
What is nobility of body?
The abandoning of the three kinds of bodily misconduct is bodily integrity; the three kinds of good bodily conduct are bodily integrity;
knowledge regarding the body as an object is bodily integrity; full understanding of the body is bodily integrity; the path accompanied by full understanding is bodily integrity;
the abandoning of desire and lust for the body is bodily integrity; and the cessation of bodily formations through the attainment of the fourth jhāna is bodily integrity.
This is bodily integrity.
What is verbal integrity?
The abandoning of the four kinds of verbal misconduct is verbal integrity; the four kinds of verbal good conduct are verbal integrity.
Knowledge regarding the object of speech is verbal refinement; full understanding of speech is verbal refinement; the path accompanied by full understanding is verbal refinement;

the abandoning of desire and lust for speech is verbal refinement; the cessation of the volitional formations of speech, which is the attainment of the second jhāna, is verbal refinement—this is verbal refinement.
What is purity of mind?
The abandoning of the three kinds of mental misconduct is purity of mind; the three kinds of mental good conduct are purity of mind;
knowledge regarding the object of consciousness is purity of mind; full understanding of consciousness is purity of mind; and the path accompanied by full understanding is purity of mind.
Mental silence is the abandoning of desire and lust for the mind; mental silence is the cessation of mental formations and the cessation of perception and feeling—this is mental silence.
“Silent in body, silent in speech, ...”
The sage whose mind is silent and free from taints, who is perfected in sagacity,
they call the one who has abandoned everything.
The Sage of body, the Sage of speech,
the Sage of mind, free from taints;
the Sage endowed with sagacity—
"They have washed away their evil," it is said.
Endowed with these three qualities of sagehood, there are six kinds of sages:
the householder sage, the homeless sage, the trainee sage, the one beyond training sage, the solitary sage, and the sage of sages.
Who are the household sages?
