Those householders who have seen the state and understood the teaching—
these are the household sages.
Who are the homeless sages?
Those who have gone forth, who have seen the state and understood the teaching—
these are the homeless sages.
The seven trainees are the sages of training.
The arahants are the sages beyond training.
The paccekabuddhas are the solitary sages.
“Sages” refers to the Tathāgatas, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
“One does not become a sage by mere silence,
being dull-witted and ignorant;”
But the wise person, having taken up the better course as if weighing it on a scale,
avoids all evil deeds.
He is a sage by that, he is a sage by that—
because he understands both worlds,
he is called a sage.
Having understood the nature of both the non-existent and the existent,
both internally and externally throughout the entire world,
one is worthy of worship by gods and humans alike.
“Having transcended the net of attachments, he is a sage.
As for “smears,” there are two smears:
the smear of craving and the smear of views... [etc.]
This is the smearing of craving... [and so on] ...this is the smearing of views.

Having abandoned the smearing of craving and relinquished the smearing of views, the sage does not smear himself, does not smear himself thoroughly, nor does he smear himself repeatedly with regard to possessions.
“Unburnt, unscorched, unsullied, gone forth, escaped, liberated, detached, he dwells with a mind free from boundaries—
the sage, amidst possessions,
is unsullied; having pulled out the arrow, he fares heedfully.”
"Arrows" refers to seven arrows:
the arrow of lust, the arrow of hatred, the arrow of delusion, the arrow of conceit, the arrow of views, the arrow of sorrow, and the arrow of doubt.
For one by whom these arrows have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed, rendered incapable of arising through the fire of knowledge—
Burnt away, he is called one who has pulled out the arrow, extracted the arrow, uprooted the arrow, completely uprooted the arrow, torn out the arrow, thoroughly torn out the arrow;
one who has abandoned the arrow, vomited out the arrow, released the arrow, relinquished the arrow, and renounced the arrow;
one who is free from craving, extinguished, become cool, experiencing bliss, and dwelling with a self that has become sublime.
With the arrow extracted.
While walking, standing, sitting, lying down, acting, behaving, protecting, maintaining, and sustaining himself;

"diligent" means one who acts with care, acts with persistence, acts with steadfastness, whose conduct is not slack, who has not cast away his desire for wholesome states, and who has not laid down his burden regarding wholesome states.
“Thinking, ‘How might I fulfill the aggregate of virtue that is not yet fulfilled,
or how might I support with wisdom here and there the aggregate of virtue that is already fulfilled,’ one applies therein desire,
effort, exertion, perseverance, non-deflection, mindfulness, clear comprehension, ardor, striving, determination, devotion, and heedfulness regarding wholesome states.”
“How might I fulfill the aggregate of concentration that is not yet fulfilled, or how might I sustain with wisdom, here and there, the aggregate of concentration that is already fulfilled...
[and so on] regarding wholesome states?
How might I fulfill the aggregate of wisdom that is not yet fulfilled?”
“May I fulfill the aggregate of liberation… or may I, through wisdom, sustain in each respective case the fulfilled aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation”—
whatever desire, effort, exertion, and perseverance there is therein.
And there is non-despondency, mindfulness, clear comprehension, ardor, striving, resolution, application, and heedfulness regarding wholesome states.
"How might I fully understand suffering that has not been fully understood? How might I abandon defilements that have not been abandoned?
How might I develop the path that has not been developed? How might I realize cessation that has not been realized?"—the desire that one has therein for this.
And exertion, effort, perseverance, fortitude, mindfulness, clear comprehension, ardor, striving,
determination, application, and heedfulness regarding wholesome states—
thus, with the arrow pulled out, one should live heedfully.
"He does not long for this world nor for the next": he does not long for this world as his own personal existence, nor does he long for the next world as another's personal existence;

he does not long for this world as his own form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, nor does he long for the next world as another's form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
he does not long for this world as the six internal sense bases, nor does he long for the next world as the six external sense bases.
He does not long for this world, nor for the world of humans; he does not long for the other world, nor for the world of devas.
He does not long for this world, the realm of sense-desire; he does not long for the other world, the realm of form or the formless realm.
He does not long for this world, the realm of sense-desire or the realm of form; he does not long for the other world, the formless realm.
One does not long for, desire, relish, yearn for, crave, or intensely pray for another destination, rebirth, rebirth-linking, existence, saṃsāra, or the round of existence; thus it is said:
"one does not long for this world or the next.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having fully understood perception, the sage crosses over the flood,
unsullied by possessions;
with the arrow extracted, he wanders heedfully.”
“He would desire neither this world nor the next.
This concludes the second exposition, the Exposition of the Discourse on the Eightfold Cave.
